Here’s a set of practical, privacy-respecting guidelines for placing cameras in an Airbnb to deter theft or vandalism, while remaining fully compliant with guest-privacy expectations and most short-term-rental policies:

1. Know the rules and be transparent  
   • Review local/state “reasonable expectation of privacy” laws and Airbnb’s camera policy.   
   • Disclose every camera in your listing description and in a welcome packet or posted house rules.  
   • Use simple signage (“Security cameras in use – see house guide for locations”) near your front door or in a communal entry.

2. Avoid private spaces  
   • Never install cameras in bedrooms, bathrooms, or any room where a guest would expect full privacy.  
   • Don’t point cameras at bedroom or bathroom windows, even from outside.

3. Exterior entry points  
   • Front door: a doorbell or fixed camera at about 7–9 ft high, angled down to capture faces but not inside the home.  
   • Back/side doors and ground-floor windows: one camera per secondary entrance, ideally at 6–8 ft to maximize field of view without capturing private interior activities.  
   • Driveway, walkway or gate: a wide-angle camera covering the approach path; helps verify who’s coming and going.

4. Outdoor common areas  
   • Pool/deck/patio: mount cameras at the far corners, elevated (8–10 ft), so they cover the entire space but not lounge chairs close-up.  
   • BBQ or fire-pit areas: one camera angled to see the overall space, not individual faces or close personal activity.

5. Indoor common rooms (if needed)  
   • Living room, dining room or kitchen: limit to 1–2 cameras placed high in corners (8–10 ft), each covering an entire wall or entryway rather than detailed close-ups of seating areas.  
   • Hallways and stairwells: cameras at each end, installed above eye-level so they can’t easily be tampered with, but positioned to see who enters/exits.

6. Technical and operational best practices  
   • No audio recording (unless you explicitly disclose it in writing and it’s legal in your jurisdiction).  
   • Use 1080p or better, wide-angle (90°–120°) lenses to reduce the need for multiple cameras.  
   • Secure your camera network: unique SSID, strong WPA2/WPA3 password, firmware updated monthly.  
   • Encrypt video at rest and in transit. Store only 14–30 days of footage unless longer retention is legally required.  
   • Enable motion-triggered alerts to reduce continuous monitoring; consider pausing indoor cameras when the home is occupied.

7. Physical installation tips  
   • Hard-mount cameras in tamper-resistant housings.  
   • Use cable management or concealment (e.g. in raceways) so wires aren’t easily cut.  
   • Keep power supplies locked or in inaccessible junction boxes.  
   • Test sight-lines in daylight and at night (with your cameras’ IR or low-light mode) to avoid blind spots.

8. Guest communication and trust  
   • In your pre-arrival email, remind guests where cameras are and why (theft deterrence, safety of children on a pool deck, etc.).  
   • Offer to disable indoor cameras upon request (with sufficient notice) or provide a privacy “off” schedule.  
   • Include a one-page diagram in your housebook showing camera locations.

By combining clear disclosure, careful placement in wholly public-area zones, proper technical safeguards and respectful guest communication, you’ll achieve effective monitoring of entries and shared spaces without infringing on your guests’ reasonable expectations of privacy.
